directAnswer: Pope Clement VI was Pierre Roger, a Benedictine theologian and celebrated preacher who reigned at Avignon from 7 May 1342 to 6 December 1352. He led the Church through the Black Death, defended Jews falsely blamed for the plague, purchased Avignon for the papacy, and set the jubilee interval at fifty years.

paras: Pierre Roger was born at Maumont in the Limousin and entered the Benedictine abbey of La Chaise-Dieu as a boy. He became a master of theology at Paris and won fame as a preacher. He served as abbot of Fécamp, then archbishop of Sens and of Rouen, and was an adviser to King Philip VI of France. Benedict XII created him a cardinal in 1338.

Elected in May 1342, he took a very different approach from his austere predecessor. He was generous toward petitioners, made his court a center of art and learning, and enlarged the Palace of the Popes with the New Palace and its great chapel.

The plague reached Avignon early in 1348 and killed a large part of the city's population. Clement stayed in the city, consulted physicians, and granted a plenary indulgence to the dying who repented. When cemeteries filled, he consecrated the Rhône so that bodies could be committed to the river.

As Jews were accused of causing the plague and massacred in many places, Clement issued bulls in 1348 forbidding violence against them. He pointed out that Jews were dying of the plague like everyone else and in regions where no Jews lived, and he ordered clergy to protect them. In 1349 he also condemned the flagellant movement that spread in the plague's wake.

In the bull Unigenitus of 1343, Clement set the interval between Holy Years at fifty years instead of one hundred, so that more of the faithful could gain the jubilee indulgence. The bull also gave a classic explanation of the treasury of merit drawn from Christ and the saints. Pilgrims came to Rome in large numbers for the jubilee of 1350, though the pope remained at Avignon.

In 1348 Clement purchased the city of Avignon from Queen Joanna I of Naples, countess of Provence, making it papal property. In Rome, he at first approved and then turned against Cola di Rienzo, who seized power in 1347 proclaiming the revival of the Roman republic.

He opposed Louis of Bavaria and supported the election of Charles IV of Luxembourg as King of the Romans in 1346. He also helped organize a naval league that captured Smyrna in 1344. Clement's lavish spending and his promotion of relatives drew criticism, including from the poet Petrarch. He died at Avignon on 6 December 1352 and was buried at La Chaise-Dieu.

keyFacts: Born Pierre Roger at Maumont; Benedictine monk of La Chaise-Dieu
Archbishop of Rouen and renowned preacher before his election in 1342
Stayed at Avignon through the Black Death (1348) and protected Jews from accusations
Set the jubilee interval at fifty years with Unigenitus (1343)
Purchased Avignon from Queen Joanna I of Naples (1348)

faqs.question: What did Clement VI do during the Black Death?
faqs.answer: He stayed in Avignon, granted a plenary indulgence to dying penitents, consecrated the Rhône for burials when cemeteries were full, and issued bulls forbidding the persecution of Jews blamed for the plague.

faqs.question: How did Avignon become papal property?
faqs.answer: Clement VI bought the city in 1348 from Queen Joanna I of Naples, who held it as countess of Provence.

faqs.question: Why was the 1350 jubilee held only fifty years after the first?
faqs.answer: In 1343 Clement VI's bull Unigenitus reduced the interval between Holy Years from one hundred to fifty years.
